questions.stem: Before inserting a urinary catheter, the nurse notices that the patient's identification band does not match the name on the procedure request. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop and resolve the identification discrepancy using approved processes before preparing the sterile field.
Ask the patient which name is correct and proceed.
Use the bed number as the second identifier.
Ask a colleague who knows the patient to confirm identity.

questions.rationale: At least two approved identifiers must match before a procedure. Familiarity, bed number or verbal reassurance does not resolve an identification discrepancy.

questions.stem: Which pair represents acceptable patient identifiers before a procedure?

options.text: Room number and diagnosis.
Full name and date of birth.
Bed number and ward location.
Photograph and procedure type only.

questions.rationale: Approved identifiers commonly include full name, date of birth or a unique medical-record number, according to local policy.

questions.stem: A patient says, 'I do not understand why this dressing change is needed.' What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: Begin because the procedure is prescribed.
Ask the family to provide consent.
Explain the purpose, main steps, expected sensations and possible discomfort, then confirm agreement.
Document that the patient is anxious.

questions.rationale: Consent requires clear information, opportunity for questions and voluntary agreement before proceeding.

questions.stem: A patient withdraws consent immediately before a non-urgent procedure. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Proceed because the equipment has been opened.
Ask another nurse to persuade the patient.
Record the procedure as refused and leave without discussion.
Stop, explore the concern respectfully and notify the appropriate clinician if needed.

questions.rationale: Consent is ongoing and may be withdrawn. The patient's concerns should be explored without coercion.

questions.stem: Before a procedure, the patient reports a latex allergy. The available kit contains latex components. What is the safest action?

options.text: Replace the kit with latex-free equipment before beginning.
Use the kit if gloves are changed.
Ask the patient whether the allergy is severe.
Proceed and observe for a reaction.

questions.rationale: Known allergies must be addressed before exposure. The correct equipment should be obtained rather than relying on monitoring after exposure.

questions.stem: Which pre-procedure assessment is most complete?

options.text: Confirm the order and gather equipment.
Review identity, consent, allergies, observations, pain, cognition, mobility, relevant results and contraindications.
Check the diagnosis and room number.
Ask whether the patient has had the procedure before.

questions.rationale: Safe preparation includes patient, procedural and environmental risks, not just technical readiness.

questions.stem: A patient is confused and unable to follow instructions for a planned transfer. What should the nurse do before beginning?

options.text: Proceed quickly before the patient becomes distressed.
Ask the patient to promise cooperation.
Reassess the assistance and equipment required and obtain additional support.
Use manual lifting to maintain control.

questions.rationale: Cognition affects transfer safety. The plan should be adjusted before movement begins.

questions.stem: Which environmental preparation best supports a safe procedure?

options.text: An open bay so staff can observe.
Equipment opened before the patient arrives.
A dim room to reduce anxiety.
A clean, private, well-lit space with equipment checked for integrity, expiry and function.

questions.rationale: The environment should protect privacy, visibility, infection prevention and equipment safety.

questions.stem: A sterile package is intact but past its expiry date. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Discard it and obtain an in-date replacement.
Use it if the contents appear clean.
Ask a second nurse to approve its use.
Use it only for a low-risk procedure.

questions.rationale: Expired equipment should not be used because sterility and performance can no longer be assured.

questions.stem: A patient reports severe pain before wound care. What is the best nursing action?

options.text: Begin quickly to finish sooner.
Assess the pain and arrange appropriate comfort or analgesia before proceeding when clinically possible.
Tell the patient some pain is expected.
Ask the patient to remain still.

questions.rationale: Pain assessment and preparation improve dignity, cooperation and procedural safety.

questions.stem: The nurse discovers that a required piece of emergency equipment is not functioning. What should happen?

options.text: Begin and replace it if needed.
Ask the patient to accept the risk.
Do not start until functioning equipment and a safe contingency are available.
Use a similar device without checking.

questions.rationale: Equipment should be checked before use, particularly when failure could delay urgent care.

questions.stem: Which action best protects privacy during an intimate procedure?

options.text: Ask visitors to look away.
Complete the procedure rapidly.
Avoid discussing privacy because it may embarrass the patient.
Close doors or curtains, expose only the required area and explain who will be present.

questions.rationale: Privacy and dignity require deliberate environmental and communication measures.

questions.stem: A nurse is unfamiliar with a procedure but has watched it previously. What is the safest response?

options.text: Seek supervision and confirm competence and scope before proceeding.
Perform it independently using the written instructions.
Ask the patient whether supervision is needed.
Delegate the procedure to an assistant.

questions.rationale: Observation alone does not establish competence. Scope and supervision requirements must be verified.

questions.stem: A patient's blood result suggests a contraindication to the planned procedure. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Proceed because the procedure is already scheduled.
Pause and seek clinical review before beginning.
Repeat the result after the procedure.
Ask the patient to decide whether the result matters.

questions.rationale: Relevant results and contraindications should be reviewed before a procedure to prevent avoidable harm.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why safety begins before equipment is touched?

options.text: Opening equipment early saves time.
Technical skill is less important than documentation.
Preparation identifies patient, consent, clinical, environmental and equipment risks before harm occurs.
Procedures are safe when prescribed.

questions.rationale: Pre-procedure checks prevent wrong-patient, allergy, consent, equipment and clinical-risk errors.

questions.stem: A patient requires an interpreter to understand a complex procedure. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Use a family member because it is faster.
Proceed using gestures.
Ask the patient to sign first.
Arrange an appropriate professional interpreter and confirm understanding before consent.

questions.rationale: Accurate communication is necessary for informed consent and safe participation.

questions.stem: A patient becomes acutely breathless while the nurse is preparing for a routine procedure. What is the priority?

options.text: Stop preparation, assess the patient and escalate according to urgency.
Complete the procedure because the equipment is ready.
Document the change and continue.
Ask the patient to rest while supplies remain open.

questions.rationale: A change in clinical condition takes priority over completing the planned task.

questions.stem: Which action is inappropriate when verifying identity?

options.text: Asking the patient to state full name and date of birth.
Using room location because the nurse knows the patient.
Comparing two approved identifiers with the record.
Resolving discrepancies before care.

questions.rationale: Room or bed location is not an approved patient identifier.

questions.stem: A patient asks a question that the nurse cannot answer within their scope. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the most likely answer.
Avoid the question.
Acknowledge the limitation and arrange clarification from an appropriate clinician.
Ask another patient who had the procedure.

questions.rationale: Honesty and appropriate referral support informed participation and professional accountability.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates safe procedural preparation?

options.text: The equipment is ready on time.
The nurse completes the checklist.
The patient has had the procedure before.
Identity, consent, risks, equipment and environment are verified before the procedure begins.

questions.rationale: Safe preparation integrates patient assessment, communication, infection prevention and equipment readiness.

questions.stem: A patient's blood pressure is unexpectedly much lower than the previous reading, and the patient reports dizziness. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Assess the patient, verify the measurement when appropriate and escalate according to urgency.
Record the result and repeat it at the next scheduled round.
Assume the cuff is faulty.
Encourage the patient to walk.

questions.rationale: Unexpected abnormal findings require prompt patient assessment, appropriate verification and timely escalation.

questions.stem: Which action improves the accuracy of a blood-pressure measurement?

options.text: Measure over thick clothing.
Use a cuff appropriate to the patient's arm size and position the patient correctly.
Use the same cuff for every patient.
Ask the patient to talk during measurement.

questions.rationale: Correct equipment size and positioning are essential for valid results.

questions.stem: A patient has an oxygen saturation of 91%, increasing respiratory effort and difficulty speaking. What should the nurse prioritise?

options.text: Repeat the saturation after one hour.
Document the value only.
Perform a focused respiratory assessment and escalate promptly.
Encourage oral fluids.

questions.rationale: The oxygen reading must be interpreted with work of breathing and functional signs; this pattern suggests deterioration.

questions.stem: Which finding belongs to a focused respiratory assessment?

options.text: Bowel sounds and urine colour.
Pupil size and grip strength.
Peripheral oedema only.
Breathing pattern, effort, chest movement and breath sounds.

questions.rationale: These are core components of respiratory assessment.

questions.stem: A pulse oximeter displays an unexpectedly low reading on a patient with cold fingers and no respiratory symptoms. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Check probe placement and perfusion, reassess the patient and repeat the reading appropriately.
Ignore the result.
Warm the device under hot water.
Document hypoxia immediately without assessment.

questions.rationale: Unexpected results should be checked for technical and clinical causes while the patient is assessed.

questions.stem: A patient becomes drowsy and diaphoretic. Capillary blood glucose is low. What is the best nursing response?

options.text: Give food immediately without further assessment.
Confirm the result, assess consciousness and swallowing safety, initiate the approved hypoglycaemia protocol and recheck response.
Wait for the medical team.
Document the value and continue observations.

questions.rationale: Treatment must reflect consciousness and swallowing safety, followed by reassessment.

questions.stem: Which neurological change requires urgent escalation?

options.text: Stable mild forgetfulness.
Chronic weakness unchanged from baseline.
A new reduction in consciousness with unequal pupils.
Normal orientation.

questions.rationale: Acute deterioration in consciousness or pupillary response may indicate a serious neurological event.

questions.stem: A patient's respiratory rate rises from 18 to 26 over two hours, although other values remain within range. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wait for a severely abnormal value.
Document the rate as normal.
Reduce monitoring to avoid anxiety.
Assess the patient, review the trend and escalate if clinically concerning.

questions.rationale: Trends and changes may indicate deterioration before a single result becomes extreme.

questions.stem: Which cardiovascular assessment finding suggests poor perfusion?

options.text: Cool extremities, weak pulse and delayed capillary refill.
Warm skin and brisk capillary refill.
Regular pulse and normal urine output.
Mild chronic oedema only.

questions.rationale: These findings suggest impaired circulation and require further assessment.

questions.stem: A patient reports severe pain but appears calm. How should the nurse respond?

options.text: Assume the pain is mild.
Accept the report, assess the pain systematically and evaluate relevant clinical factors.
Wait for visible distress.
Ask the family to confirm the pain.

questions.rationale: Pain is subjective and should be assessed using the patient's report and appropriate tools.

questions.stem: A urine specimen label has been completed away from the bedside and the nurse is no longer certain which patient it belongs to. What should happen?

options.text: Send it because the handwriting is clear.
Ask patients in the room.
Discard it according to policy and recollect using correct identification and bedside labelling.
Add the room number to the label.

questions.rationale: An uncertain specimen identity creates a serious diagnostic risk and must not be guessed.

questions.stem: Which action best supports accurate fluid-balance monitoring?

options.text: Estimate all volumes at the end of the shift.
Record only urine output.
Exclude IV fluids.
Measure and document intake and output promptly using agreed units.

questions.rationale: Timely and complete measurement improves accuracy and clinical interpretation.

questions.stem: A patient's urine output has fallen steadily over several hours. What is the best response?

options.text: Assess the patient, review fluid balance and circulation, and escalate the trend.
Wait until no urine is produced.
Encourage mobility only.
Record the total at the end of the day.

questions.rationale: Falling urine output may indicate hypoperfusion, retention or renal dysfunction and should be assessed promptly.

questions.stem: Which action is appropriate during a focused neurological check?

options.text: Measure weight only.
Assess consciousness, pupils, movement and use the relevant scoring tool.
Assess breath sounds.
Review bowel function.

questions.rationale: These findings help identify neurological change.

questions.stem: An automated blood-pressure result is inconsistent with the patient's appearance and prior trend. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Accept the device result.
Delete the result.
Reassess the patient and repeat the measurement using correct technique or an alternative method.
Wait for another nurse to notice.

questions.rationale: Clinical measurements must be interpreted in context and verified when inconsistent.

questions.stem: A patient with known diabetes has a blood glucose result outside the device's reportable range. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Record the nearest value.
Repeat it at the next meal.
Ask the patient what the value usually means.
Assess the patient, follow the device and organisational protocol, and escalate urgently.

questions.rationale: Results outside the device range may represent severe abnormality or technical error and require immediate protocol-based action.

questions.stem: Which specimen-collection principle is essential?

options.text: Use correct patient identification, container, technique, timing and documentation.
Collect first and identify later.
Use any clean container.
Leave specimens unlabelled until transport.

questions.rationale: Specimen quality and traceability depend on correct identification and preparation.

questions.stem: A patient's temperature, pulse and respiratory rate are all gradually increasing. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wait for fever above a fixed threshold.
Consider the trend clinically and assess for deterioration or infection.
Record each result separately without interpretation.
Assume anxiety.

questions.rationale: Combined trends may be more significant than one isolated value.

questions.stem: After treating hypoglycaemia, what is the next essential action?

options.text: End monitoring when the patient feels better.
Offer discharge education immediately.
Recheck blood glucose and clinical response according to protocol.
Document treatment before reassessment.

questions.rationale: Reassessment confirms whether the intervention was effective and whether further action is needed.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects competent clinical measurement?

options.text: All values are recorded.
The device produces a number.
The patient remains still.
The nurse uses correct technique, interprets results in context and acts promptly on abnormal findings.

questions.rationale: Clinical competence includes technique, interpretation and response.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: During wound care, the nurse touches a sterile key part with an unsterile glove. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Discard the contaminated item, repeat hand hygiene as needed and re-establish the aseptic field.
Continue because contact was brief.
Wipe the item with alcohol and continue.
Ask the patient whether they are concerned.

questions.rationale: Suspected contamination should be treated as contamination. Continuing would create an avoidable infection risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: Which statement about gloves is correct?

options.text: Gloves replace hand hygiene.
Hand hygiene is required at appropriate moments even when gloves are used.
Gloves are needed for every patient contact.
The same gloves may be used for several tasks on one patient.

questions.rationale: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene and should be selected according to exposure risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: What is a key part during an aseptic procedure?

options.text: Any large item on the trolley.
The patient's clothing.
A component that must not be touched because contamination could introduce microorganisms.
The outside of a waste bag.

questions.rationale: Key parts connect directly with susceptible sites or sterile fluids and must remain uncontaminated.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: An aseptic field has been left unattended. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue if nothing looks disturbed.
Ask another nurse whether anyone touched it.
Use it only for a simple dressing.
Treat the field as compromised and re-establish it.

questions.rationale: An unattended field cannot be assumed sterile.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: A patient's wound has increasing redness, pain, warmth and purulent exudate. What is the appropriate nursing response?

options.text: Assess and document the wound, follow orders and escalate possible infection.
Apply the usual dressing and review next week.
Clean the wound more vigorously.
Cover the area without assessment.

questions.rationale: The pattern suggests infection and requires objective assessment and timely review.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: Which wound documentation is most objective?

options.text: 'Wound looks bad.'
'Wound measures 3 cm by 2 cm with moderate yellow exudate and 1 cm surrounding erythema.'
'Patient is not healing.'
'Dressing was messy.'

questions.rationale: Objective documentation describes measurable findings rather than judgemental conclusions.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: A peripheral IV site is red, painful and swollen. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue using it if fluid flows.
Cover it with a larger dressing.
Stop using the site, assess it and follow the approved process for removal and escalation.
Flush it forcefully.

questions.rationale: Redness, pain and swelling may indicate infiltration or phlebitis and require prompt action.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: Which catheter-care action helps reduce infection risk?

options.text: Disconnect the drainage system routinely.
Place the drainage bag on the bed.
Use antiseptic inside the catheter daily.
Maintain a closed system, provide hygiene, secure the catheter and review ongoing need.

questions.rationale: A closed, secure and well-maintained system with early removal reduces risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: A urinary drainage bag is resting above bladder level. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reposition it below bladder level without placing it on the floor.
Leave it if urine is flowing.
Empty it into another patient's container.
Clamp the catheter.

questions.rationale: Appropriate bag position supports drainage and reduces backflow risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: Why should invasive devices be reviewed regularly?

options.text: To change them on every shift.
To confirm whether they remain necessary and remove avoidable infection risk.
To reduce documentation.
To improve appearance.

questions.rationale: Unnecessary devices should be removed promptly through approved processes.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: A nasogastric tube appears to have moved from its documented position. What should the nurse do before using it?

options.text: Push it back to the previous mark.
Ask the patient whether it feels correct.
Stop and verify placement according to policy before administration.
Use it for water only.

questions.rationale: A displaced tube can cause serious harm; placement must be verified before use.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: Which PPE selection principle is correct?

options.text: Wear maximum PPE for every procedure.
Gloves are sufficient for all exposure.
PPE is unnecessary after hand hygiene.
Choose PPE according to anticipated exposure and transmission risk.

questions.rationale: PPE should match the expected risk rather than be selected routinely or inadequately.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: A nurse performs hand hygiene, then touches a contaminated surface before accessing an IV port. What should happen?

options.text: Perform hand hygiene again and protect the key part before access.
Proceed because hand hygiene was already completed.
Wear an additional pair of gloves.
Clean the port after use only.

questions.rationale: Contact with a contaminated surface invalidates preparation for an aseptic task.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: Which finding should be included in routine device assessment?

options.text: Device brand only.
Site condition, securement, patency, hygiene and ongoing need.
Patient diagnosis only.
Date of admission.

questions.rationale: Safe device care includes local assessment, function and necessity.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: A wound dressing order is unclear. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Select the preferred dressing independently.
Ask the patient which dressing is normally used.
Clarify the order before proceeding while maintaining patient safety.
Use the most expensive product.

questions.rationale: Unclear treatment instructions should be clarified rather than guessed.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: A patient reports new severe pain at a central-line site with swelling around the neck. What is the priority?

options.text: Complete the infusion first.
Apply a warm pack.
Document and recheck at the end of the shift.
Stop the infusion as appropriate, assess urgently and escalate.

questions.rationale: Pain and swelling near a central line may indicate a serious device complication.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: Which action best maintains an aseptic field?

options.text: Arrange equipment so key parts are protected and avoid unnecessary contact.
Reach across the field repeatedly.
Allow non-sterile items to touch the edge.
Open all supplies far in advance.

questions.rationale: Planning and minimal contact reduce contamination risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: A patient with an indwelling catheter has no urine draining and reports suprapubic discomfort. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Increase the collection bag height.
Assess tubing, kinks, position and the patient, then escalate if patency is not restored safely.
Irrigate without an order.
Remove the catheter immediately.

questions.rationale: Possible obstruction or retention requires systematic assessment and policy-based action.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: Which action is safest after suspected contamination?

options.text: Continue and document it.
Use additional antiseptic at the end.
Stop, replace contaminated items and re-establish the field.
Ask a colleague to observe.

questions.rationale: Contamination should be addressed immediately, not compensated for later.

questions.sectionLabel: Infection Prevention, Aseptic Technique and Device Care
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates safe infection prevention and device care?

options.text: The procedure is completed quickly.
The dressing remains dry.
No antibiotics are prescribed.
Hand hygiene, PPE, asepsis, site assessment and ongoing device need are managed consistently.

questions.rationale: Safe care combines multiple infection-prevention and device-management principles.

questions.stem: Before giving a medicine, the nurse finds that the prescribed dose is inconsistent with the patient's renal function. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Withhold the dose and clarify the order after assessing the patient and relevant results.
Administer because the order is signed.
Give half the dose.
Ask the patient whether the dose is usual.

questions.rationale: Relevant assessment findings must be considered before administration. A potentially unsafe order requires clarification.

questions.stem: Which medication check is essential before administration?

options.text: Room number and diagnosis only.
Order, patient, medicine, dose, route, time, allergies and relevant assessment.
Medicine colour and package size.
Patient preference only.

questions.rationale: These checks form the core of safe medication administration.

questions.stem: Why should medicines be prepared for one patient at a time?

options.text: To make documentation longer.
To allow family checking.
To reduce interruptions, selection errors and patient mix-ups.
To reduce storage needs.

questions.rationale: One-patient preparation reduces cross-patient error risk.

questions.stem: A patient refuses a prescribed medicine. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hide it in food.
Record it as administered.
Ask the family to insist.
Explore the reason, provide appropriate information, notify the relevant clinician and document the refusal.

questions.rationale: A capable patient may refuse treatment; the nurse should respond without coercion and communicate the clinical implications.

questions.stem: After administering an opioid, which assessment is most important?

options.text: Respiratory rate, sedation, oxygenation and pain response.
Appetite only.
Urine colour.
Mobility only.

questions.rationale: Opioids can depress breathing and consciousness, so both benefit and harm must be monitored.

questions.stem: A patient becomes dizzy during transfer from bed to chair. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Complete the transfer quickly.
Stop, support the patient safely, call for assistance and assess observations.
Ask the patient to continue slowly.
Leave the patient standing while equipment is obtained.

questions.rationale: A change in condition takes priority over task completion.

questions.stem: Which factors should be assessed before assisting mobility?

options.text: Age only.
Diagnosis only.
Strength, balance, cognition, pain and required assistance.
Patient height only.

questions.rationale: Mobility plans should reflect physical, cognitive and safety needs.

questions.stem: A patient requires more assistance than expected during transfer. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Use manual force to complete the movement.
Ask the patient to try harder.
Lower the patient quickly to the floor.
Stop and obtain appropriate staff or equipment before continuing.

questions.rationale: The transfer plan should be revised when actual ability differs from the assessment.

questions.stem: Which action best protects staff and patient during manual handling?

options.text: Use approved equipment and techniques based on assessment.
Rely on physical strength.
Avoid explaining the transfer.
Move quickly to reduce strain.

questions.rationale: Approved handling methods reduce injury risk for both patient and staff.

questions.stem: A patient reports new pain during a procedure. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue unless the patient asks to stop.
Pause, assess the pain and decide whether to modify, stop or escalate the procedure.
Tell the patient pain is expected.
Document the pain after completion.

questions.rationale: Ongoing communication and reassessment are essential during clinical interventions.

questions.stem: Which documentation is most complete after a procedure?

options.text: 'Procedure completed.'
Equipment used only.
Assessment, procedure performed, findings, patient response and required follow-up.
The nurse's opinion of cooperation.

questions.rationale: Documentation should show what was assessed, done, found and how the patient responded.

questions.stem: When should procedural documentation be completed?

options.text: Before the intervention.
At the end of the week.
Only when an abnormality occurs.
After the intervention, as soon as practical and accurately.

questions.rationale: Records must reflect care that actually occurred and should be timely.

questions.stem: A nurse documents medication administration before giving the medicine, but the patient then refuses it. What is the main concern?

options.text: The documentation is inaccurate and may create a medication error.
The record is too detailed.
Refusal cannot be documented.
The medicine must now be given.

questions.rationale: Documentation should occur after administration and reflect the actual event.

questions.stem: A patient asks how to report dizziness during mobilisation. What is the best nursing response?

options.text: Tell the patient to wait until the transfer ends.
Explain that dizziness, weakness, pain or breathlessness should be reported immediately so movement can stop safely.
Ask the family to watch for symptoms.
Avoid discussing symptoms to reduce anxiety.

questions.rationale: Patients should know how to communicate concerns during procedures.

questions.stem: Which action best evaluates medication effectiveness?

options.text: Confirm that the medicine was swallowed.
Check the medication chart.
Reassess the intended clinical effect and monitor for adverse reactions.
Ask whether the patient likes the medicine.

questions.rationale: Administration is incomplete without evaluation of response.

questions.stem: A patient has poor balance and impulsive behaviour. Which mobility plan is safest?

options.text: Independent mobilisation to preserve autonomy.
Bed rest without assessment.
Family assistance without staff review.
Supervised mobilisation using appropriate equipment and clear instructions.

questions.rationale: The plan should address both physical and cognitive risk while preserving safe participation.

questions.stem: Which communication behaviour supports dignity during a procedure?

options.text: Explain each step, check comfort and invite questions.
Discuss the patient with staff while performing care.
Use technical language only.
Avoid eye contact.

questions.rationale: Therapeutic communication maintains involvement and respect.

questions.stem: A patient develops chest pain during ambulation. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Return the patient to bed at the planned pace.
Stop activity, support the patient, assess and escalate urgently.
Encourage deep breathing and continue.
Document the event after physiotherapy review.

questions.rationale: New chest pain during activity requires immediate assessment and escalation.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects integrated clinical skill?

options.text: Technical completion is the main goal.
Documentation can replace reassessment.
Safe care combines checks, communication, technique, observation, evaluation and documentation.
Patient comfort is secondary to task completion.

questions.rationale: Clinical skills include the judgement and communication surrounding the procedure.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates Level 1 clinical competence?

options.text: The nurse performs procedures quickly.
The nurse works without assistance.
The nurse follows technique without adapting to the patient.
The nurse prepares, performs, evaluates and documents common procedures safely and respectfully within scope.

questions.rationale: Foundational competence integrates procedural discipline, patient-centred care and professional judgement.

questions.stem: An IQN is asked to use an infusion pump model not previously encountered. What is the safest response?

options.text: Review local policy, complete supervised orientation and demonstrate competence before independent use.
Use it based on previous pump experience.
Ask another new nurse for instructions.
Decline all future infusion-pump use.

questions.rationale: Previous experience does not replace local orientation and competency verification for unfamiliar equipment.

questions.stem: Which factor should be checked before independently performing a procedure in a new healthcare system?

options.text: Whether the procedure was performed overseas.
Local scope, required supervision, approved equipment and escalation criteria.
The nurse's confidence only.
Whether the patient has had it before.

questions.rationale: Safe international practice requires confirmation of local scope, policy, equipment and supervision requirements.

questions.stem: During an OSCE, the assessor asks why the nurse checks allergies before a procedure. What is the best explanation?

options.text: It is required only for documentation.
It reassures the patient.
It identifies risks that may change equipment, medicines or whether the procedure can proceed safely.
It replaces consent.

questions.rationale: Verbalising the rationale demonstrates that the nurse understands how allergy information changes care.

questions.stem: A nurse completes every checklist step but fails to recognise that the patient is deteriorating. What does this show?

options.text: The checklist is sufficient.
The procedure should always continue.
Documentation is the only missing element.
Technical completion without clinical judgement is incomplete competence.

questions.rationale: A checklist supports consistency but does not replace assessment, interpretation or judgement.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates procedural competence?

options.text: The nurse prepares safely, performs correctly, communicates clearly, interprets findings and documents the outcome.
The nurse completes the task quickly.
The nurse follows the checklist silently.
The patient experiences no pain.

questions.rationale: Competence includes preparation, technical skill, infection prevention, communication, interpretation and documentation.

questions.stem: An unfamiliar device has a control layout different from the one used in the nurse's home country. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the controls have equivalent functions.
Request instruction and supervised practice before use.
Use trial and error on a low-risk patient.
Ask the patient whether the settings look correct.

questions.rationale: Unfamiliar equipment requires orientation because similar devices may operate differently.

questions.stem: A local policy requires a competency sign-off for a procedure the nurse has performed for years. What is the correct response?

options.text: Challenge the requirement as unnecessary.
Proceed because previous experience proves competence.
Complete the local competency process before independent practice.
Ask a colleague to sign without observing.

questions.rationale: Local credentialing requirements apply even when the nurse has previous experience.

questions.stem: Which behaviour is most professional when a nurse is uncertain about a local procedure?

options.text: Hide the uncertainty.
Proceed to maintain confidence.
Delegate the procedure without checking the other person's competence.
Seek clarification and supervision before acting.

questions.rationale: Seeking help is a professional safety behaviour, not a sign of weakness.

questions.stem: An IQN notices that local terminology differs from previous practice. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Clarify the local meaning and use approved terms in communication and documentation.
Continue using previous terminology.
Avoid documentation.
Ask patients to interpret the terms.

questions.rationale: Terminology differences can cause misunderstanding and should be resolved explicitly.

questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates safe adaptation to international practice?

options.text: Copying the procedure used in the previous country.
Relating local policy to universal safety principles while following local requirements.
Following colleagues without asking questions.
Using personal preference when policies differ.

questions.rationale: Safe adaptation combines broad safety principles with local law, policy and equipment.

questions.stem: In simulation, the nurse verbalises what would trigger escalation. Why is this important?

options.text: It shortens the station.
It replaces technical performance.
It demonstrates recognition of risk and planned clinical response.
It is needed only for examination marking.

questions.rationale: Explaining escalation criteria shows clinical reasoning beyond memorised steps.

questions.stem: A nurse is competent with one brand of device but has not used another brand. What should be assumed?

options.text: Competence transfers automatically.
Only the manufacturer is responsible.
The patient can supervise use.
Additional orientation may be required because operation and safety features may differ.

questions.rationale: Device-specific differences may affect safe operation.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports independent procedural practice?

options.text: Observed successful performance against local competency criteria.
Previous job title.
Self-reported confidence.
A colleague's informal opinion.

questions.rationale: Competence should be demonstrated, not assumed.

questions.stem: A patient deteriorates while the nurse is being assessed on a procedure. What should the nurse prioritise?

options.text: Completing the assessment station.
Stopping the procedure, supporting the patient and escalating appropriately.
Waiting for the assessor to intervene.
Finishing documentation first.

questions.rationale: Patient safety always takes priority over task completion or assessment requirements.

questions.stem: Which statement about local policy is correct?

options.text: It replaces clinical judgement.
It is optional for experienced nurses.
It guides approved practice but must be applied with patient assessment and professional judgement.
It applies only during orientation.

questions.rationale: Policy and judgement must work together.

questions.stem: A procedure is within scope but the nurse has not recently performed it. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Proceed independently.
Ask the patient to consent to the risk.
Avoid the procedure permanently.
Assess current competence and seek refresher supervision if needed.

questions.rationale: Competence must be current as well as historically demonstrated.

questions.stem: Which component is most likely to be missed if procedural training focuses only on motor steps?

options.text: Clinical interpretation and response to complications.
Equipment opening.
Hand position.
Procedure duration.

questions.rationale: International expectations emphasise judgement, rationale and response, not steps alone.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked to use a device without a local instruction manual or trained support. What should happen?

options.text: Use online information from any source.
Delay use until approved guidance or competent support is available, unless an emergency protocol directs otherwise.
Estimate the settings.
Ask another patient.

questions.rationale: Unverified device use creates avoidable risk.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of supervised practice?

options.text: To reduce the nurse's accountability.
To replace policy review.
To confirm safe performance and provide feedback before independent practice.
To allow shortcuts.

questions.rationale: Supervision supports competency development and verification.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects Level 2 adaptation?

options.text: The nurse performs familiar procedures only.
The nurse completes checklists without speaking.
The nurse avoids unfamiliar equipment.
The nurse applies local standards, explains rationales and responds appropriately to unexpected findings.

questions.rationale: Level 2 integrates adaptation, reasoning, competence and escalation.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: During an IV infusion, the patient reports burning and the site becomes swollen. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the infusion, assess the site and manage the device according to policy.
Slow the infusion.
Apply a tighter dressing.
Flush the line forcefully.

questions.rationale: Burning and swelling suggest infiltration or another complication. Continuing may worsen tissue injury.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: Which finding most strongly suggests phlebitis?

options.text: Cool pale skin around the cannula.
Redness, warmth, tenderness and a palpable venous cord.
No pain and brisk flow.
Generalised oedema.

questions.rationale: Phlebitis commonly presents with local inflammation along the vein.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: A central-line dressing is loose and damp. What is the safest response?

options.text: Reinforce it and review tomorrow.
Leave it if the line is functioning.
Replace it using approved aseptic technique and assess the site.
Remove the line without an order.

questions.rationale: A loose or damp dressing increases infection risk and requires prompt aseptic management.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: Before administering through an enteral tube, the external length differs from the documented position. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Push the tube back to the recorded mark.
Use the tube for water only.
Ask the patient if it feels normal.
Stop and verify placement according to local policy before use.

questions.rationale: A change in external length may indicate displacement and requires verification.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: Which action helps prevent catheter-associated infection?

options.text: Maintain a closed system, provide hygiene and review ongoing need daily.
Disconnect the drainage system for routine cleaning.
Keep the drainage bag above bladder level.
Irrigate routinely without indication.

questions.rationale: Closed drainage, hygiene and early removal are key preventive strategies.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: A urinary catheter stops draining and the patient reports suprapubic discomfort. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Increase the bag height.
Assess tubing, kinks, position and patient condition, then follow policy for suspected blockage.
Remove the catheter immediately.
Flush it without an order.

questions.rationale: Systematic assessment is required before intervention.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: Which wound finding requires prompt escalation?

options.text: Gradual reduction in exudate.
Healthy granulation tissue.
Increasing erythema, pain, malodour and purulent drainage.
Dry intact surrounding skin.

questions.rationale: This pattern suggests infection or deterioration.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: During an aseptic procedure, a sterile key part touches an unsterile surface. What should happen?

options.text: Continue if contact was brief.
Wipe it and continue.
Use extra antiseptic later.
Treat it as contaminated, replace the item and re-establish the field.

questions.rationale: Suspected contamination should be treated as contamination.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: A wound is not healing despite correct dressing changes. What should the nurse assess?

options.text: Wound type, tissue, exudate, infection risk, surrounding skin and wider patient factors.
Only dressing brand.
Only pain.
Only wound size.

questions.rationale: Advanced wound assessment considers local and systemic factors.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: Which action best evaluates whether an invasive device is still appropriate?

options.text: Confirm that it remains inserted.
Review the current indication, risks, function and alternatives.
Change the dressing daily.
Ask whether the patient likes it.

questions.rationale: Ongoing need should be reviewed to reduce avoidable device harm.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: A peripheral IV site is cool, pale and swollen. Which complication is most likely?

options.text: Phlebitis.
Local infection only.
Infiltration.
Normal infusion response.

questions.rationale: Coolness, pallor and swelling suggest non-vesicant fluid entering surrounding tissue.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: A vascular access device has no date or identification label. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume it was inserted today.
Use it until replacement.
Ask the patient to estimate the date.
Verify details through approved records and correct the labelling according to policy.

questions.rationale: Accurate labelling supports safe device review and accountability.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: Which practice best protects a key site?

options.text: Minimise contact and maintain aseptic non-touch technique.
Touch it with clean gloves to check sterility.
Expose it early for convenience.
Allow equipment to rest across it.

questions.rationale: Key sites should be protected from direct or indirect contamination.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: A patient develops neck swelling and breathing difficulty during central-line use. What is the priority?

options.text: Complete the infusion.
Stop use as appropriate, support airway and breathing, and escalate urgently.
Apply a cold compress.
Document and reassess later.

questions.rationale: Breathing difficulty and swelling may indicate a serious device-related complication.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: Which approach is correct when an advanced wound product is prescribed but unavailable?

options.text: Substitute any available product.
Leave the wound uncovered.
Clarify an approved alternative before application.
Ask the patient to purchase one.

questions.rationale: Prescribed products should not be substituted without appropriate clinical review.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: A nasogastric tube is used before placement is confirmed. What is the main risk?

options.text: Delayed feeding only.
Minor discomfort.
Reduced documentation quality.
Administration into an incorrect location, including the respiratory tract.

questions.rationale: Incorrect tube placement can cause severe harm.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: Which finding should be assessed before every vascular-access use?

options.text: Site condition, patency, securement and signs of complication.
Device colour only.
Patient age.
Previous shift documentation only.

questions.rationale: Direct assessment is required before and during use.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: A device complication is suspected but the prescribed therapy is urgent. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue through the compromised device.
Stop using the device and arrange safe alternative access while escalating.
Increase the rate.
Ask the patient to tolerate the discomfort.

questions.rationale: Urgency does not justify using a potentially unsafe device.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: Which documentation best supports device care?

options.text: Device present.
Dressing changed.
Site findings, patency, care performed, complications, response and ongoing need.
Patient comfortable.

questions.rationale: Detailed objective documentation supports continuity and safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Complex Aseptic Procedures and Clinical Devices
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates safe complex device care?

options.text: The procedure is technically completed.
The device remains in place.
The dressing looks clean.
The nurse confirms indication, maintains asepsis, detects complications and reviews ongoing need.

questions.rationale: Safe device care integrates assessment, technique, judgement and evaluation.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: Before a routine procedure, the patient develops new chest pain and diaphoresis. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Delay the procedure, assess airway, breathing and circulation, and escalate urgently.
Proceed quickly.
Ask the patient to sign a refusal.
Document and continue.

questions.rationale: The patient's current condition determines whether a procedure is safe to proceed.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: Which finding during a procedure requires immediate stopping?

options.text: Mild expected discomfort.
Sudden oxygen desaturation with severe coughing.
A request for more explanation.
Temporary anxiety with stable observations.

questions.rationale: Acute respiratory compromise requires immediate interruption and support.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: A patient becomes pale and less responsive during a bedside procedure. What is the priority?

options.text: Finish the procedure.
Complete documentation.
Stop, assess ABC and call for assistance.
Ask the family to observe.

questions.rationale: Changes in consciousness and colour may indicate deterioration.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: Which information is most important in an ISBAR escalation?

options.text: The entire admission history.
Only the diagnosis.
Only the abnormal observation.
Current situation, relevant background, assessment and the action or review required.

questions.rationale: ISBAR supports concise, structured escalation.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: A patient has severe coughing and desaturation during nasogastric tube insertion. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop, remove the tube as appropriate, support breathing and escalate.
Continue to complete placement.
Ask the patient to swallow harder.
Wait for saturation to recover.

questions.rationale: The notes identify this as a reason to stop rather than complete the task.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: Which action demonstrates post-procedure evaluation?

options.text: Recording that the task was completed.
Confirming the intended outcome and assessing for complications.
Discarding equipment.
Informing the next shift only.

questions.rationale: Evaluation determines whether the intervention achieved its purpose safely.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: A procedure is indicated, but current observations show severe hypotension. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Proceed because the procedure is ordered.
Ask the patient to decide.
Delay and seek urgent review because current risk outweighs immediate benefit.
Use a shorter technique.

questions.rationale: Pre-procedure judgement includes deciding whether current physiology supports the intervention.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: Which finding is expected after an uncomplicated procedure?

options.text: New severe pain and bleeding.
Reduced consciousness.
Progressive breathlessness.
A response consistent with the procedure and stable observations.

questions.rationale: Expected findings should be distinguished from signs of complication.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: A patient reports worsening pain after a procedure despite the site appearing normal. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess the patient, review the procedure outcome and escalate if unexplained or severe.
Reassure and discharge.
Document only.
Wait until visible changes appear.

questions.rationale: Pain may be an early sign of complication even before visible changes.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: What should guide the decision to continue a procedure?

options.text: The time already invested.
The patient's condition, tolerance and safety.
Whether documentation has begun.
The nurse's workload.

questions.rationale: Task completion never takes priority over patient safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects intra-procedure monitoring?

options.text: Monitor only vital signs.
Monitor after completion only.
Observe pain, breathing, colour, consciousness and overall tolerance.
Rely on equipment alarms.

questions.rationale: Ongoing clinical observation is broader than a single number or monitor.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: A patient improves after an intervention but deteriorates again 20 minutes later. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the procedure succeeded.
Wait until the next round.
Document the initial improvement only.
Reassess and escalate because the response was not sustained.

questions.rationale: A temporary response does not confirm a successful outcome.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: Which communication is most appropriate when urgent review is needed?

options.text: This is the current deterioration, these are the findings, and I need urgent review now.
The patient does not look right.
Please review when available.
The procedure was difficult.

questions.rationale: Structured escalation should state findings and required action clearly.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: A colleague gives a critical instruction during an emergency procedure. What should the receiver do?

options.text: Act silently.
Repeat the instruction back and obtain confirmation.
Wait for written documentation.
Ask another colleague later.

questions.rationale: Closed-loop communication reduces misunderstanding.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: Which finding after urinary-catheter insertion requires prompt review?

options.text: Expected mild awareness.
Clear urine flow.
No urine drainage with suprapubic pain.
Secure tubing.

questions.rationale: This pattern may indicate obstruction, misplacement or retention.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: A patient develops a rash and wheeze shortly after a procedure involving a new product. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue observation only.
Apply moisturiser.
Finish the procedure.
Stop exposure, assess ABC and activate the appropriate emergency response.

questions.rationale: This may represent an acute allergic reaction.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: Which post-procedure handover is safest?

options.text: Indication, findings, complications, response, current risks and required follow-up.
Procedure completed, patient stable.
Only the device type.
Only the time completed.

questions.rationale: Handover should make unresolved risks and actions explicit.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: When should a procedure be delayed?

options.text: Whenever the patient is anxious.
When current risk outweighs immediate benefit or required safety conditions are absent.
Whenever equipment is unfamiliar, even after training.
Whenever the nurse is busy.

questions.rationale: Delay is appropriate when safe conditions are not met.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: A procedure achieved the technical goal, but the patient developed a complication. How should success be judged?

options.text: Successful because the technical task was completed.
Successful if documented.
Incomplete or unsafe because outcome includes complications and patient response.
Successful if the patient consented.

questions.rationale: Procedural success includes both intended effect and absence or management of harm.

questions.sectionLabel: Integrating Clinical Judgement with Procedural Care
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects integrated clinical judgement?

options.text: The nurse follows the steps exactly.
The procedure is completed quickly.
The checklist is signed.
The nurse decides whether to proceed, monitors continuously and evaluates the outcome.

questions.rationale: Judgement is required before, during and after the procedure.

questions.stem: During simulation, a nurse makes an error but recognises it during debriefing. What is the main purpose of the debrief?

options.text: Identify reasoning and teamwork improvements for future practice.
Assign blame.
Repeat the station immediately without discussion.
Remove the nurse from training.

questions.rationale: Structured reflection turns simulation errors into learning without patient harm.

questions.stem: Which communication best demonstrates closed-loop practice?

options.text: Give oxygen at 10 litres.
Give oxygen at 10 litres. - Oxygen at 10 litres confirmed.
The instruction is written down.
The receiver nods.

questions.rationale: The message is repeated back and confirmed.

questions.stem: A patient with limited English needs consent for an invasive procedure. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Use a family member for convenience.
Ask the patient to sign first.
Arrange a professional interpreter and adapt information to the patient's health literacy.
Use only written English.

questions.rationale: Culturally safe consent requires accurate communication and meaningful understanding.

questions.stem: Which documentation is most complete after a procedural complication?

options.text: Complication occurred.
Doctor informed.
Patient stable.
Indication, assessment, procedure, complication, actions, response, escalation and follow-up.

questions.rationale: Professional records should show the entire clinical sequence and ongoing plan.

questions.stem: A nurse finishes a procedure but forgets to document the patient's response. Why is this significant?

options.text: The record does not show whether the intervention was effective or safe.
Response is optional.
Only the procedure matters.
The next shift can infer the response.

questions.rationale: Evaluation and response are essential components of documentation.

questions.stem: Which simulation scenario best assesses clinical judgement?

options.text: A procedure with no variation.
A procedure in which the patient deteriorates and the nurse must stop, escalate and communicate.
A written quiz only.
Equipment assembly without a patient scenario.

questions.rationale: Realistic safety challenges assess more than technical steps.

questions.stem: A critical verbal instruction is not repeated back during an emergency. What is the main risk?

options.text: The documentation will be shorter.
The patient may ask questions.
The instruction may be misunderstood or not completed.
The team may work faster.

questions.rationale: Closed-loop confirmation reduces missed or incorrect actions.

questions.stem: Which approach is culturally safe?

options.text: Assume preferences based on background.
Use the same explanation for everyone.
Ask family members to make decisions.
Ask the patient what matters, use appropriate interpretation and adapt explanations.

questions.rationale: Cultural safety depends on respectful enquiry rather than assumptions.

questions.stem: A simulation participant becomes defensive during debriefing. What should the facilitator do?

options.text: Use a respectful, psychologically safe approach focused on actions, reasoning and learning.
End the debrief.
Publicly compare performance.
Ignore the behaviour.

questions.rationale: Effective debriefing supports reflection without humiliation.

questions.stem: A nurse documents an event hours later without indicating it is a late entry. What is the concern?

options.text: The entry is too detailed.
The timing may be misleading and the record may not be transparent.
Late documentation is never allowed.
The patient must sign it.

questions.rationale: Late entries should be clearly identified according to policy.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why objective documentation matters?

options.text: It prevents all complaints.
It makes records shorter.
It supports continuity, accountability and reliable interpretation by others.
It removes the need for handover.

questions.rationale: Factual records are essential for safe shared care.

questions.stem: During a team procedure, a delegated task is not acknowledged. What should the team leader do?

options.text: Assume it will be completed.
Complete all tasks personally.
Document the omission later.
Restate the task to a named person and obtain confirmation.

questions.rationale: Named allocation and confirmation strengthen closed-loop communication.

questions.stem: A patient does not understand a written procedural leaflet. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain using plain language and teach-back, with visual or interpreter support as needed.
Ask the patient to sign anyway.
Give a longer leaflet.
Ask the family to decide.

questions.rationale: Information must be adapted to health literacy and understanding confirmed.

questions.stem: Which handover statement makes responsibility clear?

options.text: The site needs review.
The IV site is red and painful; the line is not in use, and the receiving nurse must arrange review within 30 minutes.
Please keep an eye on it.
The procedure was difficult.

questions.rationale: Specific findings, current status and required action reduce ambiguity.

questions.stem: What should be included in simulation competency assessment?

options.text: Technical performance only.
Speed only.
Preparation, communication, infection prevention, judgement, escalation and documentation.
Confidence only.

questions.rationale: Competence is multidimensional.

questions.stem: A nurse uses a family member to interpret a low-risk preference discussion. When may this still be inappropriate?

options.text: When the family member speaks the language.
When the patient is comfortable.
When the discussion is brief.
When confidentiality, accuracy or patient preference requires professional interpretation.

questions.rationale: Professional interpretation may still be needed for privacy, accuracy or sensitive information.

questions.stem: Which debriefing question best supports reflection?

options.text: What cues did you notice, what influenced your decision and what would you do differently?
Who caused the error?
Why did you fail?
Did you follow the checklist?

questions.rationale: Reflective questions explore reasoning and future improvement.

questions.stem: A nurse documents a complication but not who was informed. What is missing?

options.text: The device brand.
Evidence of escalation and continuity of responsibility.
The patient's room number.
The nurse's opinion.

questions.rationale: Documentation should show communication and follow-up.

questions.stem: Which outcome best indicates effective simulation learning?

options.text: The participant completes the station.
No errors occur.
The participant identifies learning and improves later performance and communication.
The checklist score is high.

questions.rationale: Simulation should translate into better reasoning and teamwork.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects professional Level 2 procedural communication?

options.text: The nurse speaks confidently.
The nurse uses technical language.
The procedure is completed silently.
Critical instructions are confirmed, explanations are adapted and records make risks and follow-up clear.

questions.rationale: Level 2 communication integrates closed-loop teamwork, cultural safety and professional documentation.

questions.stem: A competency assessment shows that staff can complete catheter-insertion steps correctly but often fail to respond when contamination occurs. What is the best programme redesign?

options.text: Include realistic contamination interruptions, immediate feedback and repeat practice until safe judgement is demonstrated.
Add more written theory about catheterisation.
Shorten the assessment checklist.
Allow staff to self-certify after watching a video.

questions.rationale: Competence includes judgement and response to complications, not only completion of steps. Deliberate practice with feedback targets the observed gap.

questions.stem: Which element should a comprehensive clinical-skills competency framework assess?

options.text: Technical completion only.
Knowledge, preparation, technical accuracy, communication, judgement and evaluation.
Years of experience and confidence.
Attendance at training.

questions.rationale: The notes emphasise that competence is multidimensional and cannot be reduced to a procedural checklist.

questions.stem: A learner performs a procedure correctly once during simulation. What should the educator do before confirming competence?

options.text: Sign off immediately because the steps were correct.
Ask the learner to complete a reflective paragraph only.
Assess consistency, reasoning, communication and response to complications through further supervised performance.
Rely on peer opinion.

questions.rationale: One successful performance may not demonstrate reliable competence across conditions.

questions.stem: Which feedback statement is most effective?

options.text: You need to be more careful.
You are not ready for practice.
Everyone makes mistakes.
During sterile setup, your sleeve crossed the field; pause, re-establish the field and repeat the setup now.

questions.rationale: Feedback should be specific, timely, linked to observable behaviour and followed by another practice opportunity.

questions.stem: A nurse admits uncertainty about using a device and asks for supervision. What is the most appropriate educator response?

options.text: Support the request and arrange supervised practice before independent use.
Criticise the nurse for lack of confidence.
Ask the nurse to learn by trial and error.
Remove the nurse permanently from device use.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety makes help-seeking expected and prevents unsafe independent practice.

questions.stem: Which simulation scenario best develops clinical judgement?

options.text: A predictable procedure with no interruptions.
A procedure that includes changing observations, equipment difficulty and a decision about whether to stop.
A lecture followed by a quiz.
A demonstration without learner participation.

questions.rationale: Realistic decision points and complications strengthen judgement, not just motor performance.

questions.stem: A skills educator notices wide variation in how assessors judge the same performance. What should happen?

options.text: Allow assessor preference because clinical practice varies.
Use only one assessor for all staff.
Clarify standards, use agreed criteria and calibrate assessors using shared examples.
Remove judgement from the assessment.

questions.rationale: Consistent criteria and assessor calibration improve fairness and reliability.

questions.stem: Which action best supports deliberate practice?

options.text: Completing one long simulation annually.
Reading the policy after an error.
Observing an expert without participation.
Repeated focused practice of a specific weakness with feedback and another attempt.

questions.rationale: Deliberate practice is focused, repeated and feedback-driven.

questions.stem: A learner becomes defensive after feedback. What is the best coaching response?

options.text: Return to observable behaviour, invite reflection and agree on a specific practice goal.
End the discussion.
Compare the learner with stronger colleagues.
Document failure without discussion.

questions.rationale: Constructive coaching remains specific, respectful and improvement-focused.

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of a checklist-only competency assessment?

options.text: Checklists are too difficult to score.
They may confirm task completion without assessing reasoning, communication or adaptation.
They cannot be used in simulation.
They always reduce consistency.

questions.rationale: A checklist supports consistency but does not replace judgement.

questions.stem: A nurse repeatedly performs well in simulation but poorly during busy shifts. What should the educator investigate?

options.text: Whether simulation should be abandoned.
Whether the nurse prefers another specialty.
Transfer of learning, workload, interruptions, supervision and real-world conditions.
Only the nurse’s motivation.

questions.rationale: Performance is shaped by both competence and workplace conditions.

questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates an effective skills programme?

options.text: High attendance.
Positive course evaluations only.
Completion of every checklist.
Consistent safe performance, appropriate help-seeking and improved patient outcomes.

questions.rationale: Training should translate into reliable practice and safer care.

questions.stem: A mentor observes that a nurse understands theory but hesitates during complications. What is the best next step?

options.text: Use supervised complication scenarios with guided reasoning and feedback.
Provide more reading.
Sign off theory competence only.
Avoid exposing the nurse to complexity.

questions.rationale: The identified gap is applied judgement under changing conditions.

questions.stem: Which environment most strongly supports learning?

options.text: One in which errors are hidden.
One in which uncertainty can be discussed without humiliation while standards remain clear.
One in which only experts speak.
One in which every error leads to punishment.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety supports honest learning and early help-seeking.

questions.stem: A competency programme uses the same assessment for novice and advanced nurses. What is the main concern?

options.text: The programme is too efficient.
All learners should be assessed identically.
Assessment may not match role, risk or expected level of judgement.
Advanced nurses need no assessment.

questions.rationale: Competency processes should align with role and clinical risk.

questions.stem: Which action best develops assessors?

options.text: Allow assessors to rely on intuition.
Rotate assessors frequently without preparation.
Use only self-assessment.
Train assessors, compare scoring decisions and review difficult cases together.

questions.rationale: Assessor preparation and calibration improve consistency.

questions.stem: A learner makes an error during simulation that would have harmed a patient. What should the educator do?

options.text: Use debriefing to examine reasoning, system factors and a safe repeat performance.
End the learner’s programme immediately.
Ignore it because no patient was harmed.
Focus only on technical correction.

questions.rationale: Simulation allows errors to become structured learning opportunities.

questions.stem: Which teaching method is strongest for a high-risk skill?

options.text: A recorded lecture only.
Demonstration, supervised practice, realistic simulation, feedback and reassessment.
A policy acknowledgement form.
Informal peer observation.

questions.rationale: High-risk skills require multimodal practice and verified performance.

questions.stem: A nurse performs safely but cannot explain critical safety rationales. What should the assessor conclude?

options.text: Competence is complete because performance was correct.
The rationales are irrelevant.
Further assessment is needed because understanding supports adaptation to unexpected events.
Only documentation needs improvement.

questions.rationale: Verbalised reasoning helps confirm that safe actions can be adapted beyond memorised steps.

questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects Level 3 leadership in clinical-skills education?

options.text: The nurse personally performs every complex procedure.
The nurse replaces simulation with policy review.
The nurse assesses technical speed only.
The nurse builds reliable competency systems that develop judgement, feedback and safe help-seeking.

questions.rationale: Level 3 leadership strengthens the capability of others and the learning system.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Procedural Safety Systems
questions.stem: Repeated specimen-labelling errors occur because labels print away from the bedside and several patients have similar names. Which intervention is strongest?

options.text: Introduce bedside label printing, barcode verification and a redesigned workflow.
Remind staff to check labels carefully.
Increase annual education.
Ask patients to inspect their labels.

questions.rationale: Workflow redesign and forcing functions are stronger than reminders alone.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Procedural Safety Systems
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects human-factors thinking?

options.text: Competent staff should never make mistakes.
Systems should reduce reliance on perfect memory, attention and concentration.
Training removes all risk.
Errors are mainly caused by poor motivation.

questions.rationale: Human performance is limited, especially under fatigue and interruption.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Procedural Safety Systems
questions.stem: A medication-preparation area is frequently interrupted. What is the strongest control?

options.text: Tell nurses to focus.
Add a reminder poster.
Redesign the area and workflow to reduce interruptions during high-risk tasks.
Ask nurses to prepare medicines faster.

questions.rationale: Environmental and workflow redesign is stronger than relying on vigilance.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Procedural Safety Systems
questions.stem: Which recommendation is weakest after a procedural incident?

options.text: Standardise equipment layout.
Introduce forcing functions.
Redesign confusing labels.
Tell staff to be more careful.

questions.rationale: General reminders are weak controls because they rely on memory and attention.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Procedural Safety Systems
questions.stem: Why should frontline staff participate in learning reviews?

options.text: They understand how work is actually performed and where pressures or workarounds occur.
They can identify who is to blame.
They replace data analysis.
They should write all recommendations.

questions.rationale: Frontline insight helps reveal practical system conditions.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Procedural Safety Systems
questions.stem: A review blames one nurse for using the wrong connector but ignores two nearly identical connectors stored together. What is missing?

options.text: A competency checklist.
Analysis of equipment design and storage as contributing system factors.
A disciplinary response.
Patient education.

questions.rationale: Systems thinking examines conditions that shaped the error.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Procedural Safety Systems
questions.stem: Which control is strongest in the hierarchy of controls?

options.text: Annual education.
A warning label.
A connector design that makes incorrect attachment physically impossible.
A reminder email.

questions.rationale: Forcing functions and engineering controls are stronger than administrative reminders.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Procedural Safety Systems
questions.stem: A procedure kit contains different items on each ward. What is the most appropriate improvement?

options.text: Ask staff to memorise local differences.
Use larger labels only.
Allow each ward to continue its preference.
Standardise kit contents and layout across the service where clinically appropriate.

questions.rationale: Standardisation reduces variation and omissions.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Procedural Safety Systems
questions.stem: A new checklist increases completion time and staff begin bypassing it. What should leaders do?

options.text: Review usability, workflow impact and whether the checklist targets meaningful risks.
Punish every bypass.
Add more checklist items.
Stop measuring bypasses.

questions.rationale: Workarounds may signal poor design and should prompt evaluation.
